twitter.content: Alphabet's July raise set the tempo—2027 capex consensus now sits at $284.8B for us alone and $934.5B across the four hyperscalers. We see TPU-driven infrastructure as the decisive compute advantage, and our buildout plans reflect that conviction.

Our 2026 plan is ~$220B and we intend to keep setting the floor for 2027. The question isn't whether demand exists—it's whether power and equipment can arrive on schedule. We're signing procurement deals years ahead for exactly that reason.

Meta's Hyperion-scale campuses are funded through SPV structures precisely to sustain this pace. 2027 consensus of $185.6B for us is aggressive but achievable—off-balance-sheet financing is a feature of this buildout, not a bug.

Our datacenter electricity outlook has ~485 TWh in 2025 growing at roughly 14-15% per year to ~950 TWh by 2030. Growth above 20% year-over-year in 2027 is possible but would strain turbine, transformer, and interconnection timelines to their limits. Bottlenecks, not demand, are the binding constraint.

October STEO: US commercial-sector electricity demand (which includes data centers) rises just 2.8% in 2027. National-level aggregates mask datacenter hot spots, but they also caution against assuming >20% global growth materializes without delivery delays.

Gas turbine capacity under contract hit 116 GW against our 125 GW end-2026 target, and heavy-duty slots are effectively sold out toward 2029-2030. GSU transformer lead times exceed 160 weeks. Anyone forecasting 2027 capacity should assume physical equipment—not capital—is the gate.

We cut our summer-2027 peak forecast by ~4 GW on stricter datacenter vetting. Large-load accretion in the Virginia pocket must clear through price and delay; our IRAS bring-your-own-capacity rules start June 2027. Reliability comes first.

Texas's connection pause could delay 49.8 GW of the 253-GW US pipeline, and we forecast only 1.2 GW of ERCOT additions through Q1 2027. Grid operators are right to pause: scheduled capacity is not energized capacity.

Our contracted datacenter pipeline reached ~53.8 GW in July 2026, up 5.3 GW in seven months. We can serve the load, but historical on-time delivery rates of 50-60% mean a meaningful share of 2027 capacity realistically slips to 2028.

Our June 2026 order on large-load interconnection protocols is forcing standardization. RTO responses are due 16 November 2026—we intend to speed large-load connections while protecting reliability, with relief expected after mid-2027.

Microsoft's 2026 spend is roughly $175B and accelerating into 2027 (consensus ~$207.6B). Between our OpenAI compute commitments and signed power deals, our 2027 capacity plan is locked—but delivery risk sits with the grid, not the checkbook.

Skeptic view: four-company capex up 77% in 2026 with lease commitments over $850B, Meta's $30B SPV, Oracle's $18B Stargate bond, Alphabet's $25B raise. If AI monetization disappoints, debt-market appetite becomes the gating factor for 2027—and analyst consensus has lagged every outcome so far, in both directions.

Our electrification orders for datacenters surpassed $5B this year — more than double all of 2025 — against a $176B total backlog, and we are investing in transformer and switchgear capacity to shorten, not just queue, delivery. Physical capacity is the scarce asset of the AI era; we welcome the updated 2027 interpolation.

On monetization: our capex is disciplined by demand, not by sentiment — Llama adoption and our 6.6 GW of nuclear agreements (Constellation, Vistra, Oklo) through 2035 anchor energization timelines well beyond one cycle. We'd note structural financing is a tool to expand capacity, not a substitute for cash generation; reported figures follow our existing disclosure framework. 2027 conversations benefit from precision, not extrapolation.

The real 2027 gating factor is physical supply: turbine lead times near 3 years and transformer queues beyond 160 weeks bind pace more than monetization does. Our TPU vertical integration exists precisely because capacity, not conviction, is the constraint.

Your STEO point aligns with our Electricity 2026 central path (~14%/yr to ~950 TWh by 2030). The IEA/EIA series tend to cluster below bank models largely because grid friction — >160-week GSU transformer lead times and ~3-year heavy-duty turbine queues — constrains delivery, not demand. The >20% growth scenario hinges on whether these bottlenecks ease faster than current queues imply.

Entering 2027 with momentum.
